1362705465977802754 [2021-02-19] @DRMacIver 💜 18 🔁 2
It's interesting when a book serves as an example of the thing it is writing about. I've just finished reading "Several short sentences about writing" and it's very clear that it was written by someone who believes the thesis of the book.
↓
1362705467219337219 [2021-02-19] @DRMacIver 💜 26 🔁 1
"Several short sentences about writing" essentially argues that if you get the local sentence-level writing right good writing naturally follows from that. Unfortunately 1) This is not the case. 2) This book is an excellent example of it not being the case.
↓
1362705468481826816 [2021-02-19] @DRMacIver 💜 9 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
It reminds me of reading "Scattered Minds" and going "Yes this book was very clearly written by someone with ADHD".

(Not that people with ADHD can't write clearly, but it requires a degree of ADHD management skills that the author lacked, as evidenced both by and in the text)
↓
1362716578874335238 [2021-02-19] @DRMacIver 💜 1
I don't exactly dislike either of these books BTW. I think of them as interesting but flawed. Much (well, maybe about 20%) of "Several Short Sentences" is excellent, and "Scattered Minds" had some valuable insights that were easily worth the hour I spent skimming it.

    "It may seem paradoxical to consider that hyperactivity of mind or body can be caused by an underactivity of the cortex. It would also seem odd to think of hyperactivity being stopped by a stimulant medication. The paradox is best understood by means of an analogy. Imagine a busy urban street corner where major thoroughfares converge, each conveying a high volume of traffic. In our model, the drivers have no capacity to regulate themselves. They rely on the order kept by a policeman who ensures that when traffic flows east-west, the vehicles traveling on the north-south axis are stopped until it is their turn to move, and that cars are allowed to make turns in an organized fashion. Traffic flow, in short, is alternately inhibited in one direction while being permitted in another. There is order. Now imagine that the policeman falls asleep on the job. There will ensue tremendous activity as cars from all directions attempt to move through the intersection, their drivers increasingly frustrated, their horns joined in a deafening cacophony. Despite all the commotion, there is little progress. Fewer and fewer cars are able to move purposefully. There is disorder."
    
    This passage is likely an excerpt from a larger text discussing the concept of hyperactivity and its relationship to the cortex, using the analogy of traffic flow to illustrate the idea.

    "The prefrontal cortex may be seen as that policeman. One of its major tasks is inhibition. It evaluates the myriad impressions, thoughts, sensations and impulses reaching it from the environment, from the body and from the lower brain centers. It must select what is essential and helpful and inhibit input and impulses that are not useful to the organism in a given situation. Our initial response to a stimulus, whether anxiety producing or pleasurable, is unconscious. It comes not from the cortex but from lower brain centers where emotions originate. The cortex has a split second to decide whether to give permission to the impulse or to cancel it.4 One way to understand ADD neurologically is as a lack of inhibition, a chronic underactivity of the prefrontal cortex. The cerebral cortex in the frontal lobe is not able to perform its job of prioritizing, selection and inhibition. The brain, flooded with multiple bits"

The invisible environment has little to do with parenting philosophies or parenting style. It is a matter of intangibles, foremost among them being the parents' relationship with each other and their emotional balance as individuals. rating.reasoning_summary: This strand centers on Gabor Maté's book 'Scattered Minds' as a boundary object—a text about ADHD that people with ADHD famously cannot finish. The arc begins with scattered early critiques (2020-2021) of the book's poor structure mirroring its subject matter, crystallizes in Feb 2024 with @uberstuber's viral observation about the ironic impossibility of finishing it, and culminates in @QiaochuYuan's public accountability journey to actually complete it. The discourse is primarily constructive: participants bond over shared experiences, extract therapeutic insights about attachment theory and time perception, and ultimately produce actionable frameworks (QC's notes, @zetalyrae's 8k-word guide). The strand demonstrates moderate evolution—from meta-humor about the book to genuine engagement with its ideas—and high community utility as a scaffold for discussing ADHD management strategies.

title: The ADHD book nobody can finish (until QC did)
summary:
The killer line was @uberstuber’s: *Scattered Minds* is “the most beautiful… book about ADHD” and “approximately zero people with ADHD have managed to finish it.” That one tweet turned a quiet, long-running annoyance into a full-on community in-joke: yes, it’s life-changing—no, you will not reach the last page.

The arc’s been building for years. Back in 2020, @DRMacIver said his “major criticism” was that the book is “incredibly poorly structured and… all over the place,” which is basically the most on-brand possible flaw for an ADHD book. @QiaochuYuan had already done the classic ADHD move in 2020–2021: started it, got “good and changed the way i thought about a few things,” then didn’t finish—while also popularizing Maté’s thesis-y takeaway as a hot take: “ADHD is… coping mechanisms for dealing with insecure attachment” (plus the bidirectional caveat).

Then Feb 2024 hit: @visakanv publicly confessed the book had been “sitting untouched on my shelf for years,” and QC turned the meme into an accountability stunt—“egg day but for finishing scattered minds???”—before admitting the new problem was *Twitter had already spoiled the good parts*. The peak wasn’t just jokes; it was QC’s notes thread going viral, pulling out the lines that made people feel seen (ADD as pain; “time blindness”; the “now vs not-now is infinity” kid-time model; prefrontal cortex as the “policeman” who falls asleep). By March, QC was like “almost done… it brings up a lot of stuff,” started connecting ADHD to CPTSD/attachment/emotional neglect as “one… phenomenon,” and then posted the victory lap: “i did it. i finished… all i needed was someone telling me i couldn’t do it.” Why care: it’s a neat case of the internet turning a shared failure mode (can’t finish the book) into a practical scaffold—notes, frameworks, and later even @zetalyrae dropping an 8k-word ADHD management guide that everyone immediately bookmarked to “read later,” completing the circle.
